---
title: "Rust library interface"
---

This document describes the design of the functions forming the Rust library and
tracks the implementation status. All of these functions are external-facing
functions that are used internally in the [CLI](cli.qmd) commands.

{{< include /docs/includes/_design-status.qmd >}}

## {{< var planned >}} `Rap`

This struct contains everything needed for later functions by bundling `Package`
and `Request` structs together. It's called `Rap` as an acronym for "Request And
Package". Nearly all internal functions make use of this struct.

## {{< var planned >}} `read_package()`

This function reads in the data package's metadata file (currently only the
`datapackage.json` file) into a `Package` struct. While we called it `source` in
the args of many CLI commands, we call it `package` here to be clearer. "Source"
on it's own is a vague term, "source of what?", so we wanted to be explicit that
it is the data package's metadata we are reading in. Plus, the struct is called
`Package`. However, the `read_package()` has the argument called `source`, which
is the location given in the `SOURCE` arg of many of the CLI commands.

At some point we aim to support other metadata formats, but for now only
[`datapackage.json`](https://datapackage.org) is supported.

The signature is (with an internal `PackageSource` enum for the different source
locations):

```text
read_package(source: PackageSource) -> Result<Package, Error>
```

## {{< var planned >}} `read_request()`

This reads in the `request.yaml` file into the `Request` struct. This
functionality is very similar to `read_package()`. The signature is:

```text
read_request(path: &str) -> Result<Request, Error>
```

## {{< var planned >}} `check_request()`

The `check_request()` function takes the `Rap` struct that contains the
`Request` and `Package` data and outputs whether any checks failed. It takes
ownership of `Rap` in order to consume it as later functions shouldn't use this
object anymore. The output is a set of errors that indicate the problems if
there as a failure, otherwise, outputs a `CheckedRap` object to indicate it has
been checked. See the diagram below for an overview of what is going on
internally. Once we start implementing it we'll know how to group and organize
these errors.

<!-- TODO: Update design once we learn more about errors in Rust. -->

The approximate signature is:

```text
check_request(rap: Rap) -> Result<CheckedRap, Error>
```

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-cap: "The flow of input and output through the `check_request()` function."
%%| fig-alt: >-

%%|   function. The user bundles the request and package structs into a Rap
%%|   struct, which is input into `check_request()`. The function completes a
%%|   set of checks, before returning a result that's either the unit type
%%|   (nothing) or a set of errors.

flowchart TD
    request[/"Request"/]
    package[/"Package"/]
    rap[/"Rap"/]
    output[/"Result\< CheckedRap, Errors \>"/]

    subgraph check ["check_request()"]
      check_package_name["check_package_name()<br>Package name matches metadata"]
      check_package_version["check_package_version()<br>Package version matches metadata"]
      check_resource_names["check_resource_names()<br>Resource names match metadata"]
      check_column_names["check_column_names()<br>Column names match metadata"]
      check_row_filters["check_row_filters()<br>Row filters match metadata columns"]
    end

    request & package --> rap

    rap -->
      check_package_name -->
      check_package_version -->
      check_resource_names -->
      check_column_names -->
      check_row_filters -->
      output

    check:::outer_function
    classDef outer_function fill:none
```
